column5: na'budu; Hebrew la'avod; walk all his ways
column6: Joshua joins serving YHWH with walking all his ways; Hebrew avad is cognate with the commentary's na'budu, making its service-and-road equation concrete.

column5: obey, be my people, walk the commanded way
column6: Jeremiah makes obedience and walking the commanded way the condition of belonging to God, clarifying the commentary's owned servant who addresses the true master.

column5: Abraham goes onward to worship
column6: Abraham's worship is expressed as a journey with a promised return, a precise counterpart to the commentary's claim that worship and the traversed way are one action.

column5: level path of your feet
column6: Proverbs tells the walker to level the track under his feet, directly supplying the commentary's image of feet making a road surface straight and firm.

column5: prepare YHWH's way; make a highway straight
column6: Isaiah's prepared, straight desert highway gives a scriptural form to the requested sirat as a route made ready for the divine encounter.

column5: Way of Holiness; walkers do not go astray
column6: The highway is explicitly contrasted with going astray, matching the commentary's straight communal road and its lost alternative.

column5: this is the way; walk in it; right or left
column6: A guiding voice gives the traveller the exact formula and directional correction developed in the commentary's guide who goes before the wayfarer.

column5: led by streams on a straight, non-stumbling path
column6: Jeremiah combines a gathered people, water, divine leading, a straight path, and freedom from stumbling in one verse.

column5: continual guidance, thirst satisfied, watered garden
column6: Isaiah binds guidance to provision in dry ground, closely meeting the commentary's route, water, need, and nurturing Lord.

column5: make me know your ways; teach me your paths
column6: This direct prayer for taught paths is a close liturgical companion to ihdina al-sirat.

column5: instruct and teach the way to go
column6: The speaker promises personal instruction and counsel about a particular way, giving a biblical analogue to the hadi who guides a traveller.

column5: hand leads and right hand holds
column6: The psalm makes being led and physically held together, illuminating the commentary's traveller supported while he walks.

column5: I hold your right hand; I help you
column6: YHWH's direct promise to hold the hand and help gives concrete form to the worshipper's request for assistance.

column5: teach me to do your will; lead me on level ground
column6: Prayer for obedience and for the good Spirit to lead on level ground links voluntary service, help, and an upright route.

column5: for your name's sake lead and guide me
column6: The psalm joins the divine name to being led and guided, sharpening the commentary's movement from a naming sign to a requested way.

column5: build up the highway; lift a signal for peoples
column6: Isaiah places a raised signal and a cleared communal road in the same command, matching the commentary's opening sign and constructed path.

column5: YHWH's house, taught ways, walked paths
column6: The nations go to a house so that they may learn and walk God's paths, giving the commentary's road both a community and a destination.

column5: level ground so Israel may walk safely
column6: Baruch makes the leveling of mountains and valleys serve Israel's safe walking, a close late-Jewish parallel to the straight road's communal movement.

column5: trees shade Israel at God's command
column6: The commanded shade gives a direct textual companion to the commentary's road, water, and shade cluster.

column5: God leads Israel with mercy and righteousness
column6: The closing promise combines divine leading, a people on the move, mercy, and righteousness in the terms developed around rahim and guidance.

column5: trust, help, make your ways straight
column6: Sirach joins reliance on God, promised help, and straightened ways in a compact form that closely mirrors the fifth and sixth ayat's prayer.

column5: bless God and ask that your ways be made straight
column6: Tobit's instruction makes blessing the Lord and asking for straight paths one devotional practice, matching the commentary's praise-to-guidance movement.

column5: ways of truth and perversity; peace or wrath
column6: The Rule of the Community develops two opposed ways whose outcomes are peace or divine wrath, supplying a precise Second Temple counterpart to the two faces of losing the path.

column5: two ways of life and death
column6: The opening Two Ways instruction gives a Christian communal formulation for the commentary's straight route and its opposed lost route.

column5: YHWH goes before to lead them by the way
column6: The pillar goes before Israel specifically in order to lead them on the journey, a direct analogue for the guide preceding the traveller.

column5: God goes before to find a place to camp
column6: Deuteronomy depicts God travelling ahead to locate the people's resting place, adding a destination to the commentary's forward-leading guide.

column5: take my yoke; learn from me; find rest
column6: Jesus turns the animal yoke into willing discipleship and rest, directly meeting the commentary's tamed servant and weary traveller.

column5: my yoke is easy and my burden light
column6: The easy yoke and light burden give a concrete Christian counterpart to submissive service that does not crush the one who seeks help.

column5: make straight paths for your feet; the lame be healed
column6: The command retains both the physical track made by feet and the contrast of injury with restored upright movement.

column5: guide our feet into the way of peace
column6: Zechariah's hymn gives the guide the precise task of directing feet into a saving way.

column5: narrow way leading to life
column6: The contrast of a life-giving way with another route gives an explicit Christian form to the commentary's road with two divergent endings.

column5: forsook the straight way and went astray
column6: Second Peter uses the paired language of a straight way and straying, directly matching the commentary's upright walker and dallin.

column5: Father's house as destination
column6: Jesus describes the Father's house as the destination prepared for his people, illuminating the commentary's road that has a final home.

column5: I am the way to the Father
column6: The way is identified with the mediator who brings people to the Father, a direct Christian meeting of route, guide, and home.

column5: kept from stumbling and made to stand
column6: Jude pairs divine preservation from falling with standing before glory, exactly reversing the commentary's falling under wrath.

column5: serve not for the sake of reward
column6: Avot distinguishes service for reward from service freely given to the master, clarifying the commentary's contrast between coerced slavery and chosen worship.

column5: freed from sin and enslaved to God
column6: Paul's paradox of liberation into God's service gives a sharp Christian analogue to voluntary servitude under the true owner.

column5: free people, yet servants of God
column6: The verse expressly holds freedom and God's service together, directly illuminating the commentary's freely chosen kul.

column5: Israelites are my servants, brought from Egypt
column6: Leviticus opposes Egyptian bondage to belonging as God's servants; Hebrew avadim is cognate with Arabic abd and makes the true-owner contrast explicit.

column5: Egyptians ruthlessly made Israel serve
column6: Exodus supplies the forced enslavement that the commentary sets against Moses's willing service to the real Rabb.

column5: Israel is God's firstborn son
column6: Calling enslaved Israel God's son places divine parenthood over Pharaoh's claimed control, sharpening the false-nurturer and true-Rabb contrast.

column5: Moses's mother nurses him for Pharaoh's daughter
column6: Where the Qur'anic Pharaoh presents upbringing as a claim upon Moses, Exodus makes his own mother the nurse and Pharaoh's daughter the payer.

column5: Pharaoh's daughter takes and names Moses
column6: Exodus assigns adoption and naming to Pharaoh's daughter, a significant alternative to Pharaoh himself claiming to have reared Moses in his household.

column5: Pharaoh's daughter takes Moses and raises him
column6: Stephen retells the royal adoption in the same terms that frame the commentary's Pharaoh-and-Moses dispute.

column5: Moses refuses to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son
column6: Hebrews interprets Moses's adult choice as rejection of the royal identity, reinforcing the commentary's contrast of imposed palace status and chosen allegiance.

column5: Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well
column6: The verse fixes the journey and the well that the commentary gathers into Moses's guided road-and-water scene.

column5: Midian's daughters draw water and fill troughs
column6: The source scene explicitly joins the well, women drawing water, and troughs for a flock.

column5: Moses helps the women and waters their flock
column6: Moses's intervention at the well culminates in watering another's flock, the direct biblical parallel to the commentary's scene.

column5: the women return to their father's house
column6: The return home after the well episode adds the household destination that the commentary gives to the road and sacrificial herd.

column5: camels kneel by a well as women come to draw water
column6: The servant's journey joins camel, well, water, and a household-seeking mission in a single scene.

column5: Rebekah draws water for the camels
column6: Water is given to the traveller's animals as well as the traveller, a close counterpart to herd, need, and guidance meeting at the well.

column5: YHWH led me on the way to my master's kin
column6: The servant explicitly credits God with leading him on a route to a household, closely matching guide, owner, way, and home.

column5: Jacob rolls the stone and waters Laban's flock
column6: Jacob's well scene conjoins a journeying relative, water, a flock, and movement into a household as Moses's Midian scene does.

column5: water for feet and rest under a tree
column6: Abraham's hospitality gives travelling visitors water and shade, an exact meeting of two images developed in the commentary.

column5: Abraham takes a tender calf from the herd
column6: The animal from the herd is selected for a household offering of hospitality, paralleling the commentary's separated herd-animal brought to a home.

column5: Abraham serves food under the tree
column6: Serving guests under shade joins willing service, food, and shelter in the Abrahamic setting beside the commentary's route-and-need imagery.

column5: Judge of all the earth does justice
column6: Abraham's appeal to the Judge of all the earth gives a biblical analogue to Rabb al-alamin and the day when justice is rendered.

column5: I am dust and ashes before the Lord
column6: Abraham's self-description before judgment supplies a concrete biblical face-to-dust counterpart to the commentary's humiliated, fallen side of the day.

column5: God will provide the lamb for the offering
column6: Abraham's answer makes the sacrificial animal God's provision, linking herd, divine name, and the journey to worship.

column5: Jesus, wearied by travel, sits at Jacob's well
column6: The scene makes a tired traveller, a road, and a well coincide, closely matching the commentary's Moses cluster.

column5: YHWH is my shepherd; I lack nothing
column6: The shepherd relation gives the herd a known owner whose care answers the commentary's ownerless animal and needy traveller.

column5: green pasture and waters of rest
column6: The shepherd's grazing place and waters give a close biblical form to the flock's going out and returning around water.

column5: he leads me in right paths
column6: The same shepherd restores and guides on right paths, fusing herd leadership and the straight road.

column5: shepherd gathers, carries, and gently leads the flock
column6: The tender leader of the flock gives a strong counterpart to hadi as both guide and herd-leader.

column5: no hunger or thirst; guide them to springs
column6: The promised guide supplies water and relief from need, directly meeting the commentary's travel, thirst, and leading.

column5: unknown owner, animal kept at home until restored
column6: The law expressly imagines not knowing an animal's owner and bringing it home until it can be returned, a close legal counterpart to the ownerless camel.

column5: lost sheep; seek your servant
column6: The speaker is simultaneously a strayed sheep and God's servant who asks to be sought, tightly joining dallin, herd, and worship.

column5: lost sheep led astray by their shepherds
column6: Jeremiah's people are lost sheep whose leaders turned them from their resting place, directly meeting wrong guidance, herd, and home.

column5: seek lost, bring back strayed, bind injured
column6: The divine shepherd's actions reverse loss, falling, and weakness in the terms developed across the commentary's way and herd images.

column5: shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out
column6: The sheep's known name, owner, and being led out directly counter the commentary's animal whose master is unknown.

column5: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow his voice
column6: The shepherd's going before the flock is a precise Christian analogue to the guide ahead of both traveller and herd.

column5: I know my own and my own know me
column6: Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep intensifies the commentary's final contrast between known ownership and the animal cut off from its owner.

column5: seek the one lost sheep until he finds it
column6: The search for the strayed sheep gives the commentary's lost animal a returning shepherd and a deliberate homeward movement.

column5: straying sheep returned to Shepherd and Overseer
column6: First Peter explicitly turns straying into return to a shepherd, a direct Christian parallel to dallin and guided recovery.

column5: sheep without a shepherd
column6: Jesus reads an unguided crowd through the exact herd-and-leader image the commentary develops for hadi.

column5: the Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
column6: The Lamb who is also shepherd fuses sacrificial animal, herd leader, and water-guidance in an eschatological form.

column5: all who enter the world pass before God for judgment
column6: The Mishnah makes universal judgment resemble a passing flock, closely joining the commentary's herd image to the day of reckoning.

column5: horse or mule restrained by bit and bridle
column6: The psalm's undisciplined animal needing restraint provides a direct counter-image to the commentary's tamed camel and willing servant.

column5: YHWH is shade at your right hand
column6: The divine keeper as shade on the traveller's side gives a compact biblical counterpart to the commentary's shade and sustaining help.

column5: clouds, rain, and grass on the hills
column6: The psalm explicitly has God nourish vegetation through cloud and rain, matching the commentary's nourishing Rabb.

column5: rain, fruitful seasons, food from heaven
column6: Paul's speech identifies the Creator through rain, crops, and food, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's clouds and plants nourished by the Rabb.

column5: Hebrew rachem, womb, and compassion
column6: Isaiah joins a nursing child, a mother's womb, and rachem; that Hebrew root is cognate with the commentary's rahim and supplies its maternal-mercy image.

column5: my name forever; my memorial for generations
column6: God's self-naming gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's beginning with a name that identifies the owner.

column5: called by name; you are mine
column6: Being called by name and declared God's own directly answers the commentary's contrast between recognized ownership and the masterless animal.

column5: put my name on Israel and bless them
column6: The priestly formula treats the divine name as a mark of belonging and blessing, illuminating name, sign, and completed favor.

column5: bring offerings to the place where YHWH's name dwells
column6: The verse brings sacrifice, divine name, and a chosen dwelling together, closely matching the commentary's herd-animal, spoken name, and home.

column5: lamb taken according to each household
column6: The Passover instruction joins a selected flock-animal to a household, offering a concrete biblical counterpart to sacrifice brought home.

column5: luminaries for signs and seasons
column6: Genesis calls the heavenly lights signs rather than gods, directly serving the commentary's distinction between a sign and what it signifies.

column5: Abraham looks at counted stars as promised descendants
column6: Genesis gives Abraham's star-gazing a covenantal meaning rather than a test of a celestial lord, a meaningful alternative to the commentary's night scene.

column5: sun, moon, and stars must not be bowed to or served
column6: The warning against serving the host of heaven is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's sun-worshippers who mistake sign for Rabb.

column5: sun shining and moon moving in splendor
column6: Job names the very visual appeal of sun and moon that makes the commentary's ascending celestial signs a test of discernment.

column5: heart secretly enticed; hand kissed in worship
column6: The next verse identifies the move from seeing luminaries to idolatrous devotion, making explicit the error the commentary assigns to sun-worship.

column5: sun, moon, stars, and heavenly lights treated as gods
column6: Wisdom lists the celestial bodies people mistake for rulers of the world, an unusually close Jewish parallel to the commentary's Abrahamic scene.

column5: creator perceived from the greatness of created things
column6: The argument from visible beauty to the Maker directly articulates the commentary's rule that a sign is not the thing it signals.

column5: host of heaven worships its maker
column6: Nehemiah reverses astral worship: the heavenly host itself worships YHWH, so celestial things become servants rather than lords.

column5: people worship the sun toward the east
column6: Ezekiel supplies a concrete scene of sun worship, the precise failure the commentary describes when rising things are treated as Rabb.

column5: heavens declare God's glory
column6: The heavens function as proclamation of God rather than as God, giving a concise biblical form to the sign-and-signified distinction.

column5: served the creature rather than the Creator
column6: Paul makes the inversion of worship explicit, directly matching the commentary's warning against taking a created heavenly sign for its Lord.

column5: earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, and stars say they are not God
column6: Augustine stages the commentary's distinction in first-person form: visible creatures direct the seeker beyond themselves to their maker.

column5: YHWH our judge, lawgiver, king, and savior
column6: Isaiah gathers judge and king in one confession; Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary's Malik, while the verse joins ownership to deliverance.

column5: wicked will not stand in the judgment
column6: Hebrew qum, to stand, is cognate with the commentary's qama, and the verse places that standing exactly in the judgment scene.

column5: Aramaic dina, court seated, books opened
column6: Daniel's Aramaic dina is cognate with the commentary's din; court, books, and the assembled host make its day-of-reckoning image especially close.

column5: Hebrew yadin judges the world in righteousness
column6: The Hebrew d-y-n verb gives the dīn root a judicial use while its object is the whole world, matching din and alamin.

column5: weighed in balances and found lacking
column6: Daniel turns the balance into a verdict on a king, directly meeting the commentary's scale and judgment-day imagery.

column5: just balances and just weights
column6: The Torah's command makes an unbent balance an ethical demand, supplying the legal ground for the commentary's warning about deficient measure.

column5: false balance and just weight
column6: The proverb sets deceitful scale against the weight God delights in, sharpening the commentary's moral reading of the mizan.

column5: make the ephah small and the shekel great; falsify scales
column6: Amos supplies the concrete market fraud behind the commentary's scene of those who cheat in measure before the Lord of worlds.

column5: let God weigh me in just balances
column6: Job asks for divine weighing that will disclose integrity, directly pairing balance with the final moral account.

column5: measured waters and heavens; weighed mountains in scales
column6: Isaiah places sky, waters, and scales in one divine act, a close counterpart to the commentary's meeting of heaven and balance.

column5: all things arranged by measure, number, and weight
column6: Wisdom makes cosmic order a matter of measure and weight, directly enlarging the commentary's scale from commerce to the worlds.

column5: deed written, sealed, witnessed, and weighed out
column6: Jeremiah's purchase preserves writing, seal, witnesses, money, and duration together, closely paralleling the commentary's debt-document scene.

column5: two or three witnesses establish a matter
column6: The law's witnesses make a legal matter stand, directly illuminating the commentary's witness, forgetting, and uprightly established writing.

column5: credit, open ledger, writing hand, collectors, true judgment
column6: Avot's shop-and-ledger parable unites debt, recorded accounts, payment, and a true judgment in the exact cluster developed in the commentary.

column5: three books opened at the new-year judgment
column6: The Talmud's books for righteous, wicked, and intermediate persons make the judgment day an explicit written accounting.

column5: some awaken to life and some to shame
column6: Daniel's resurrection divides the outcome of the final scene into honor and shame, matching the commentary's contrasting faces on the day.

column5: wise shine like the brightness of the sky
column6: The shining righteous after judgment supplies a biblical counterpart to the softened or radiant face set against dust and disgrace.

column5: righteous stand with great confidence
column6: The righteous standing before their former oppressors closely matches the commentary's upright figure set against those who fall under wrath.

column5: they go astray in heart and do not know my ways
column6: The psalm explicitly combines straying, ignorance of God's ways, and the divine response later called wrath.

column5: in my wrath they shall not enter my rest
column6: The oath of wrath gives the opposite destination to the guided flock's place of rest.

column5: way of wicked is darkness; they do not know what makes them stumble
column6: Proverbs makes lost direction visible as a walker who stumbles without knowing why, closely matching the commentary's fallen wayfarer.

column5: crooked paths; walkers do not know peace
column6: Isaiah's crooked paths and absence of peace provide a direct Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's route that bends away from guidance.

column5: day of wrath and righteous judgment
column6: Paul's phrase directly joins wrath to an appointed judicial day, the pair the commentary gathers around din.

column5: God fixed a day to judge the inhabited world
column6: Paul's Areopagus speech gives the judgment day a universal scope, closely corresponding to the Lord of the worlds.

column5: all appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due
column6: The verse treats final judgment as recompense owed, a precise Christian counterpart to din as a day of settled debt.

column5: dead stand, books open, judged by recorded deeds
column6: Revelation combines standing persons, opened books, and individual judgment, the central visual cluster of the commentary's day.

column5: hide from the face of the enthroned one and the Lamb's wrath
column6: The terrified call for mountains to fall over them gives an exact Christian image of wrath, faces, and falling.

column5: the great day of wrath has come; who can stand
column6: The verse explicitly sets wrath's day against the ability to stand, matching the commentary's fall-versus-upright contrast.

column5: all nations gathered and separated as sheep from goats
column6: The final judgment is staged as a shepherd's sorting of animals, directly meeting herd imagery and the day of account.

column5: sheep on the right and goats on the left
column6: The bodily arrangement of the flock makes the judgment's two outcomes spatial, complementing the commentary's two ways of being lost.

column5: cursed depart into eternal fire
column6: The king's adverse verdict supplies an explicit Christian judgement-and-wrath counterpart to the angry path's end.

column5: stand upright and lift your heads at redemption
column6: Jesus's command gives the positive posture opposed to the commentary's face-down falling under wrath.

column5: they always go astray and have not known my ways
column6: Hebrews carries the Psalm's language of straying and unknown ways into a Christian warning.

column5: they shall not enter my rest in my wrath
column6: The next verse retains wrath and denied rest, sharpening the commentary's opposed destinations.

column5: the measure used is measured back
column6: The same measure becomes judicial reciprocity, a compact Christian counterpart to balance and account.

column5: give account on the day of judgment
column6: Jesus explicitly uses the language of rendering an account on the final day, closely meeting the commentary's debt-and-record imagery.

column5: a king settles accounts with his servants
column6: The parable puts king, servants, debt, and reckoning in one scene, directly paralleling Malik, abd, and the day debt is closed.

column5: settle with an accuser while on the way to the magistrate
column6: Luke makes the road itself the place to resolve a debt before judgment, an unusually close meeting of path, debt, and day.

column5: record of debt with legal demands erased
column6: Paul's cancelled written debt gives a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's written obligation and its final settlement.

column5: each gives an account of himself to God
column6: The individual account to God directly maps the commentary's day when every person stands before the Lord of worlds.

column5: black horse holds a balance scale
column6: The apocalyptic balance makes measure part of a judgment sequence, extending the commentary's mizan into a Christian final-day image.

column5: our Father; hallowed be your name
column6: The Lord's Prayer opens with a named, direct address to God, closely accompanying the commentary's movement from divine name to second-person devotion.

column5: give us today our daily bread
column6: The shared prayer moves from address to requested provision, matching the commentary's needy traveller and nurturing Lord.

column5: forgive us our debts
column6: The petition uses debt to name what requires divine resolution, directly accompanying the commentary's din-and-borrowing imagery.

column5: do not lead us into trial; deliver us from evil
column6: The final petition asks not to be led into a destructive course and for rescue, closely paralleling help and the requested right way.

column5: God's servants worship before the throne
column6: The final city presents uncoerced service before the true ruler, a culminating Christian counterpart to na'budu.

column5: they see his face and bear his name
column6: The named servants see God's face in the final home, reversing the commentary's faceless loss, wrath, and unknown ownership.

column5: distinguish one who serves God from one who does not
column6: Malachi makes service to God the criterion separating two destinies as judgment approaches, closely matching the commentary's willing servant and two outcomes.

column5: children enslaved because of debt
column6: Nehemiah joins debt to forced enslavement in a concrete social scene, illuminating the commentary's juxtaposition of debt and coerced servitude.

column5: I will lead slowly according to the livestock's pace
column6: Jacob's journey places a leader ahead of children and nursing flocks, supplying a specific pastoral bridge to the commentary's guide, herd, and tired traveller.

column5: living water given at the well
column6: At the traveller's well, water becomes a divine gift; this extends the commentary's physical water-and-need scene into John's symbolic register.

column5: the community called the Way
column6: Acts turns a communal allegiance into the name of a way, a specific but non-narrative counterpart to the commentary's path joined to a people.

column5: benei maron read through sheep or a narrow pass
column6: The Talmud's interpretations of the Mishnah's procession make individual passage before the judge resemble either a flock or a constricted route, joining herd, path, and judgment.

column5: Abraham's anti-idol argument in Terah's workshop
column6: The midrash recasts Abraham's discernment of false gods as a contest with made images, extending the commentary's sign-versus-Lord distinction.

column5: Abraham teaches one creator rather than celestial powers
column6: Josephus interprets Abraham as arguing from the ordered cosmos to one creator, a close historical reception of the commentary's astral scene.

column5: Moses refuses Egyptian nurses and is nursed by his mother
column6: The tradition makes Pharaoh's household dependent on Moses's own mother for his nurture, intensifying the commentary's challenge to Pharaoh's claim of upbringing.

column5: Moses thought his brothers would understand his deliverance
column6: Stephen supplies a positive intention for Moses's intervention among the oppressed, an interpretive counterpoint to the commentary's self-description as among the lost.

column5: Wisdom enters the servant of the Lord against dread kings
column6: Wisdom portrays Moses as God's servant confronting royal power, giving a late-Jewish bridge between the commentary's true Rabb and Pharaoh's coercion.

column5: records, weighing, and judgment of souls
column6: The apocalypse's judgment tableau gathers written records, scales, and verdicts, a close later-Jewish expansion of the commentary's balance-and-account scene.

column5: look to him, become radiant, faces not ashamed
column6: The psalm's radiant, unashamed faces give a specific positive counterpart to the commentary's contrasting faces, though outside its final-judgment setting.

column5: no one can serve two masters
column6: Jesus's master-servant saying supplies a focused Christian bridge between worship, ownership, and the commentary's contrast of true and false masters.

column5: offering drawn from cattle or flock
column6: Leviticus supplies the sacrificial category of herd and flock behind the commentary's animal separated for an offering, without its full homeward scene.

column5: root of Jesse as a signal sought by nations
column6: The raised signal draws a people toward a resting place, a secondary biblical bridge to the commentary's sign, path, and communal destination.
